Chapter 9: Addressing Power Dynamics and Intersectionality
You know, no relationship happens in a bubble where everyone’s on totally equal footing. Power dynamics—they show up everywhere. Think about things like gender, race, class, ability, or even age. All of these shape how we connect with each other, and that includes relationships outside the traditional, monogamous mold.
If you really want to build ethical, equitable connections, it’s so important to notice and address these dynamics. Sometimes, power sneaks in quietly—like who usually starts the tough conversations, whose needs seem to come first, or who simply has more social pull or financial resources.
In non-monogamous setups, you might notice even more layers. Maybe there’s a hierarchy between primary and secondary partners. Or maybe someone’s just way more experienced or comfortable with non-traditional relationships, and that shifts the balance.
Here’s where intersectionality comes in. It’s the idea that all our identities—like our race, sexuality, gender, and more—overlap and shape our experiences. So, the challenges and opportunities a queer person of color faces in a non-monogamous community? They’re not going to be the same as those for a straight, white, cisgender friend. It’s a reminder that there’s no one-size-fits-all.
So, what can you do about all this? Here are a few practical steps:
First, awareness. Check in with yourself—how do privilege and power show up in your relationships or your circles? Sometimes just noticing is the first real step.
Next, practice active listening. Make real space for voices that don’t always get heard. And be ready for feedback, even if it’s hard to hear.
Then, work on equitable agreements. Make sure everyone gets a say in decisions. Agreements shouldn’t just be handed down by whoever has the most power.
And finally, keep up with ongoing education. Learn about privilege, oppression, social justice—then use what you learn to improve how you relate to others.
Here’s a quick example. Imagine a group where one person’s needs always seem to take priority. What if the group paused and said, “Hey, let’s look at our agreements and see how we can create more balance”? Or maybe a community decides to go out of its way to welcome and support folks from all sorts of backgrounds.
By facing power dynamics and intersectionality head-on, you’re not just making relationships more ethical—you’re making them fair, inclusive, and way more authentic. When people feel truly seen and valued, trust grows deeper, and the connections you build become so much richer.
